questions.question: Wrte a note on any 2 pricing methods. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Note on any 2 Pricing Methods: Cost Plus Pricing : Selling Price = Unit Cost +
  • Fixed Profit Margin - ensures all costs are covered and profit is guaranteed - Example:
  • Cost ₹100 + 20% mark-up → ₹120. Value Based Pricing : Price is set base d on
  • customer’s perceived value - used for premium or differentiated products - Example:
  • Apple iPhone pricing. Competition Based Pricing : Price is fixed by analysing
  • competitor prices - useful in markets with similar products - Example: Telecom plan
  • pricing. Geographic Pricing : Different prices for different regions or locations -
  • reflects transport cost, taxes, or local demand - Example: Higher prices in metro
  • cities. Promotional Pricing: Temporary price reductions to boost sales - used during
  • festivals or clearance periods - Example: Diwali sale discounts. Freemium Pricing :
  • Basic version free; advanced features paid - common in digital products and apps -
  • Example: Spotify free vs. premium.

questions.question: Explain any 2 types of pricing. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Any 2 Types of Pricing: Penetration Pricing: Low initial price to enter the market
  • quickly - helps attract customers and gain market share - Example: New OTT
  • platform offering ₹99/month. Price Skimming: High initial price, then gradually
  • reduced - used for inno vative or new technology products - Example: New
  • smartphone launch. Psychological Pricing: Prices set to influence perception (e.g.,
  • ₹999 instead of ₹1000) - makes the product appear cheaper - Example: Retail clothing
  • stores. Premium Pricing: High price to signal superior quality or exclusivity - used by
  • luxury brands - Example: Rolex watches. Bundle Pricing: Multiple products sold
  • together at a combined lower price - encourages customers to buy more - Example:
  • Fast food combo meals. Dynamic Pricing: Prices change based on demand, time, or
  • conditions - common in travel and online platforms - Example: Uber surge pricing.

questions.question: Differentiate between wholesalers and Retailers. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Difference between Wholesalers and Retailers: Wholesalers are intermediaries who
  • purchase goods in large quantities directly from manufacturers and sell them in bulk
  • to retailers, industrial users, or other wholesalers - typically operate from warehouses,
  • focus on volume based transactions, and do not usually deal with final consumers -
  • primary functions include bulk breaking, storage, financing, and risk bearing.
  • Retailers are intermediaries who purchase goods from wholesalers or manufacturers
  • and sell them in small quantities directly to final consum ers - operate close to the
  • consumer market, provide customer service, offer product variety, and play a key role
  • in influencing consumer buying decisions - focus on convenience, display, after sales
  • service, and personal selling.

questions.question: What are the '4A's' of rural marketing? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• 4As of Rural Marketing: 1. Affordability: Products must be priced to suit rural
  • income levels – companies offer low -unit packs, value pricing, and cost -efficient
  • products to ensure purchase feasibility. 2. Availability/Accessibility: Products reach
  • remote and geographically dispersed rural areas - requires strong distribution
  • networks, village‑level entrepreneurs, and innovative last‑mile delivery systems. 3.
  • Awareness: Focuses on educating rural consumers about the product’s benefits, usage,
  • and value - companies use local communication channels such as wall paintings, folk
  • media, village events, and mobile vans. 4. Acceptability: Designing products that
  • meet rural needs, preferences, and cultural expectations - includes product size,
  • packaging, durability, and relevance to rural lifestyles - companies adapt offerings to
  • local tastes and conditions.

questions.question: What factors influence promotion mix decisions? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Factors influencing Promotion Mix Decisions: Promotion mix is the combination of
  • promotional tools such as advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public
  • relations, direct marketing, etc. that are shaped by several internal and external factors
  • - Any three valid factors: nature of the product (Consumer goods (FMCG) require
  • mass advertising and sales promotion becau se they target a large audience, w hile
  • industrial goods require personal selling because buyers need techni cal information
  • and negotiation) – nature of the market/target audience (A large, geographically
  • dispersed market requires ad vertising and digital promotion, w hile a small,
  • concentrated market may rely more on personal selling) – stage in the product life
  • cycle (Introduction stage: Heavy advertising and sales promotion to create awareness
  • - Growth stage: Competitive advertising to build preference - Maturity stage: Sales
  • promotions to defend market share - Decline stage: Minimal promotion) – budget
  • availability (Firms with lar ge budgets can i nvest in mass media advertising, w hile
  • firms with limited budgets rely on cost‑effective tools like digital marketing or
  • personal selling) – competition intensity (In highly competitive markets, firms must
  • invest more in advertising, sales promotions, and brand‑building activities to
  • differentiate themselves. While in low‑competition markets, minimal promotion may
  • be sufficient) – organisation-related factors (Company size, reputation, marketing
  • objectives, and internal capabilities influence promotional decisions. Large firms may
  • use all promotional tools, while smaller firms may focus on selective methods)

questions.question: How do buying motives influence consumer decisions ? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Buying Motives influence Consumer Decisions: Buying mot ives are the internal
  • forces that drive a consumer to purchase a product. They explain why a consumer
  • chooses one product over another. According to consumer‑behaviour research,
  • motivation is the “spark” that triggers purchase decisions and v aries widely a cross
  • individuals. Buying motives therefore play a central role in shaping consumer
  • choices.
  • a. Rational motives : Rational motives are based on logical thinking and
  • objective evaluation.
  • How they influence decisions:
  • - Consumers compare price, quality, durability, utility, and performance.
  • - They choose products that offer the best value for money.
  • - Leads to careful, well‑planned decisions.
  • Example: Buying a laptop based on RAM, processor speed, and warranty.
  • b. Emotional motives: Emotional motives arise from feelings such as pride, fear,
  • love, joy, comfort, or status.
  • How they influence decisions:
  • - Encourage impulse buying.
  • - Create strong brand attachment.
  • - Influence purchases in luxury, fashion, and lifestyle categories.
  • Example: A consumer buys a premium perfume to feel confident or attractive.
  • c. Social motives: Consumers buy products to gain acceptance, recognition, or
  • belonging in society.
  • How they influence decisions:
  • - Shape lifestyle choices and brand preferences.
  • - Peer influence and social approval guide many purchases.
  • - Particularly strong among youth.
  • Example: Buying branded shoes or smartphones to fit in with friends.
  • d. Loyalty motives: These motives explain why consumers prefer certain shops
  • or brands.
  • How they influence decisions:
  • - Trust, good service, convenience, and reputation lead to repeat purchases.
  • - Consumers remain loyal even when alternatives exist.
  • - Builds long‑term customer relationships.
  • Example: A consumer shopping at a supermarket known for its cleanliness
  • and quality.
  • Buying motive s – rational, emotional, social, and loyalty – play a crucial role in
  • shaping consumer decisions. They determine how consumers evaluate products, select
  • brands, and make final purchases. Understanding these motives helps marketers
  • design effective strategies that appeal to customer needs and emotions.

questions.question: "Distribution channels are crucial for marketing success." Explain. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Distribution Channels are crucial for Marketing Success: Distribution channels
  • are the pathways through which goods move from producers to consumers. They
  • include wholesalers, retailers, agents, distributors, and online platforms. They play a
  • vital role in ensuring that products are available, accessible, and delivered efficiently.
  • a. Ensures Product Availability : Distribution channels make sure products
  • reach the right place at the right time. Even the best produ ct fails if it is not
  • available when customers want it. Example: FMCG companies rely on
  • extensive retail networks to ensure daily‑use products are always in stock.
  • b. Reduces Distribution Costs : Intermediaries perform essential functions such
  • as transportatio n, storage, financing, and risk‑bearing. This reduces the
  • producer’s burden and lowers overall distribution costs. Efficient channels
  • minimise wastage, delays, and handling expenses.
  • c. Expands Market Reach : Distribution channels help companies reach
  • geographically dispersed markets, including rural and remote areas. This
  • increases sales volume and market penetration. Example: Hindustan Unilever
  • Limited (HUL)’s rural distribution network reaches thousands of villages.
  • d. Enhances Customer Convenience: Retailers, supermarkets, and e‑commerce
  • platforms provide easy access, variety, and after‑sales service. Convenience
  • improves customer satisfaction and encourages repeat purchases. Consumers
  • prefer brands that are readily available.
  • e. Supports Promotion and Branding : Channel partners participate in in‑store
  • displays, merchandising, demonstrations, and promotions. This increases
  • brand visibility and influences buying decisions at the point of sale. Retailers
  • often act as brand ambassadors.
  • f. Facilitates Market Feedback : In termediaries provide valuable information
  • about consumer preferences, competitor activities, and market trends. This
  • helps producers adjust pricing, packaging, and promotional strategies.
  • Distribution channels are essential for marketing success because th ey ensure product
  • availability, reduce costs, expand reach, support promotion, and improve customer
  • satisfaction. Without efficient distribution, even the best products cannot succeed in
  • the market.
